title: Quadratic Reciprocity
short: For odd primes p ≠ q, (p/q) = (q/p), except when p ≡ q ≡ 3 (mod 4), when (p/q) = −(q/p).
trouble: Students flip a symbol whose top number is not an odd prime (factor it first), or forget the minus sign when both primes are 3 mod 4.

blocks.html: Here are two questions that seem unrelated: is $13$ a square mod $47$? Is $47$ a square mod $13$? Gauss proved, as a teenager, that the answers are linked by a simple sign rule. He called it the golden theorem and gave several different proofs of it. With it and the supplementary laws, any Legendre symbol shrinks quickly, much like the Euclidean algorithm.

The law of quadratic reciprocity. For distinct odd primes $p$ and $q$, $$\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)\left(\frac{q}{p}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \cdot \frac{q-1}{2}}.$$ In words: $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)$, unless $p \equiv q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, in which case $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = -\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)$.

The exponent $\frac{p-1}{2} \cdot \frac{q-1}{2}$ is odd only when both factors are odd, that is, when $p \equiv q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$; that is where the minus sign comes from. The proof is beyond this lesson (one classical proof counts the lattice points under the diagonal of a $\frac{p}{2} \times \frac{q}{2}$ rectangle in two ways), but its power is easy to see: after flipping, the top number can be reduced mod the new bottom, so the numbers keep getting smaller until the supplementary laws or $\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = 1$ finish the job.

items: Reduce the top mod the bottom.
Factor the top. Drop squared factors; handle $-1$ and $2$ with the supplementary laws.
For each odd prime on top, flip with reciprocity (minus sign if both are $3 \bmod 4$), and repeat.

blocks.html: Flipping a symbol whose top is not an odd prime. "$\left(\frac{15}{17}\right) = \left(\frac{17}{15}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{15}\right)$, and 2 is not a square mod 15, so the answer is $-1$" is wrong: 15 is not prime, so the law does not apply to it, and the true value is $\left(\frac{3}{17}\right)\left(\frac{5}{17}\right) = (-1)(-1) = 1$. Factor the top into primes first. And when both primes are $3 \bmod 4$, do not forget the minus sign.

Reciprocity also answers "for which primes $p$ is 3 a square?" in one stroke: $\left(\frac{3}{p}\right) = 1$ exactly when $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{12}$. (Try $p = 11$: $5^{2} = 25 \equiv 3$.) A version for composite bottoms, the Jacobi symbol, is left for a later course.
For distinct odd primes, $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)$ unless both are $3 \bmod 4$, when there is a minus sign. Reduce, factor, flip, repeat.
